en: The banner in her hand,
From her king, Lord Manas,
Which eighty-year-old Chyiyrdy
Held as the gift he left—
Each time she looked, her hunger was sated.
He had no companion but his mother,
No strength to gird himself.
The old lady made him her support;
She had no other people besides him.
Before the old woman,
She turned her face toward the Truth.
The lawful livestock left by Manas—
Before the old lady
She offered the wether as a gift.
The two ladies dipped their hands in water,
Performing ablution of their hands;
They dipped their feet in water,
Performing ablution of their feet.
To slaughter the brown wether
The two ladies made ready.
In former days, your dear sister-in-law Kanykei,
When she was the fairest of women,
The youngest of twelve daughters,
A servant beloved of God,
In the gardens of great Bukhara,
When she played there,
Still a little girl herself,
Her hair not yet long enough to braid,
Had saddled her white winged steed.
The glorious, sacred Quran
She had read as a girl.
The surah called Tappat
She read with astonishing speed;
The Quran's Kulkuldabat
She recited fittingly from memory.
Spreading her palms, hastening,
To Manas, gone to the other world,
To his spirit, as two meals' worth,
She dedicated the brown wether.
The mottled-necked Ak Tinte
She drew out of its sheath.
Your precious sister-in-law Kanykei,
Her eyes shining like a camel calf's,
One part of the white blade's handle
She had her orphan Semetey hold.
As a ritual, the brown wether—
She slaughtered the brown wether now.
Committing its soul to Allah,
Your sister-in-law Kanykei
Cut off its head.
When all their wealth was scattered,
Your mountainlike mother Chyiyrdy,
The infant still of cradle age
Clasped against her breast,
Running toward the hills,
Despairing of her precious life,
When she fled this way,
Your lion mother Chyiyrdy
A merciless calamity
Had brought upon them indeed!
'If anything appears, I shall slaughter it,
And give my orphan one full meal,' she had said.
The little cauldron left by Manas
Your mother had brought along!
The stand and stones for the hearth
She set out ready now.
Dry firewood giving off no smoke—
Your exhausted sister-in-law Kanykei
Gathered it on the plain.
Beseeching her Allah,
All the brown wether's meat
She put in, leaving nothing out.
Your capable mother Kanykei,
Cooking it in no time,
Brought it to a vigorous boil.
The hind shank and meat of the hip,
The finest of all the joints,
She gave to her mother Chyiyrdy.
Its thick fat tail, big as a cauldron,
She gave to Semetey.
The neck meat with its bones
Quickly stirred his appetite.
He was still an infant of cradle age,
Just six months old.
The famished Semetey,
The brown wether's fat tail—
When he pulled at it from one side,
Gulping it every which way,
Sucking at it back and front,
Nothing could be seen when they looked.
The brown wether's fat tail—
Where it had gone, no one could tell.
The soft flesh of the ribs,
When they placed it in the orphan's hand,
He sucked that out of sight as well.
Your dear mother Kanykei
For the orphan and the widow
She kindled their extinguished fire,
Brought their deadened souls to life,
Joined what had been severed,
Kindled their extinguished fire,
Gathered what had been scattered.
Kanykei, built like a warrior,
Weeping ceaselessly and hastening,
That cradle infant Semetey
Against the front of her overskirt
She settled in his swaddling clothes.
Then, saying these words,
She held him, distraught,
Beseeching her mother Chyiyrdy:
'Mother, whom I cherish,
Has endless night fallen on our heads?
Mother, whom I cherish,
Turning toward Karakan,
The day has come for us to flee!
What shall we do by staying here?
Taking the only child as our support,
Come, let us wander away to Temir Khan!
Let us flee to Karakan;
The only child left by my khan Manas,
Mother, let us take for our companion.
When he reaches twelve years old,
Let us send an army into Talas.
If God grants it, upon those slaves
Let us avenge our unforgotten wrong!
Mother, if his thoughts reach far,
If he has a long life,
This child the fierce wolf left behind,
I shall take your camp away from Keng-Kol.
When my orphan reaches twelve,
If I live, I shall take revenge upon those slaves.
I shall seize my Sart in Talas.
Mother, if I see Talas on my return,
Mother, I shall drive out
Your bitterest anguish.
Mother, turn your thoughts to nothing else.
Let us go, taking as our refuge
The child your hero left behind.
We were of royal birth; let us prove worthy.
Putting kingship out of mind,
Until your child reaches twelve,
Let us depend upon my birth family.
Mother, let us leave, not stay here.
Come, let us reach a place we know!
Mother, our lives are clothed in mourning;
Only a spoonful of our blood remains.
If we recall what has passed,
Mother, our souls will burn away.
If our strength fails, mother,
Let us die where it gives out.
If the mighty spirit of the sultan supports us,
The only child the generous one left—
Let us try to carry him away.
Walking and moving until we die,
Mother, let us die upon our hurried way.
The hoof the winged steed left behind,
Mother, the little one, a peerless charger,
Until death, against our breasts like this,
Let us hold him as we go to meet our death.
We were a gorge; we have become a road.
We were of royal birth; we were abased.
We were a surging Ala-Köl;
We became mud for cattle to wade through.
We were plane trees; we were felled.
Mother, we were a dense forest; we were thinned.
Mother, we were silken thread; we became wool.
Together losing our only one,
We consumed our fortune.
Mother, we were white winged steeds; we wasted away.
You were the pure, venerable lady;
I was the pure young wife.
Mother, suffering anguish, we grew old.
You were a royal old woman;
Mother, I was khan over them all.
The days of blessing left our royalty;
For your daughter-in-law Kanykei
The day of grieving has arrived.'
Then the old woman of eighty years,
The holy woman who bore Manas,
The old lady stood and said:
'O Kanykei, my little foal,
Now that my temple hair is white,
With my final journey awaiting me,
Parted from my countless riches,
How shall I wander to Samarkand?
I was a vast lake fed by rivers;
How shall I settle in a riverbed?
Leaving my own people, Kanykei,
How shall I live among the Sarts?
O Kanykei, my little foal,
Now that my beard is white,
With my final journey awaiting me,
By remaining alive, without dying,
What desire could I fulfill?
The Six Cities, the khan of Kokand,
And Margilan at the far end—
What shall I do, wandering there?
Parted from a people with a royal court,
When I go among those people,
My little foal, what desire could I fulfill?
For my ruined self,
Kanykei, do not shoot harriers for me to eat.
With my head of true royal birth,
If I go there in ruin,
Do not let them call me a wretched woman!
O Kanykei, my little foal,
For my destitute self,
Do not shoot ruddy shelducks for me to eat.
Parted from my son the khan,
Do not let them call me a wandering crone!
Without distressing my soul,
My cherished Kanykei,
Set out for Bukhara yourself.
It is God's command.
If you will not take offense,
Leave wretched me right here!
O Kanykei, my little foal,
Let me endure my suffering.
Beside my precious, matchless falcon,
O Kanykei, my little foal,
Let me lie with our feet together.
O Kanykei, my little foal,
Leaving the wheat here,
What desire could I fulfill?
For Manas, greater than other men,
O Kanykei, my little foal,
Let me give myself in sacrifice.
Ah, Kanykei, my little foal,
Let me set together with the moon.
Beside my precious morning star Manas,
Here in this very place,
My little foal, let me lie with our feet together.
O Kanykei, my little foal,
If you flee to Samarkand, set out.
Do not make an old woman like me wander;
Leave me in this very place.
Do not torment an old woman.
O Kanykei, my little foal,
Do not trouble my soul.
'My mother was left in the open wilds'—
Kanykei, do not divide your thoughts with that.
Kanykei, I entrust him to you:
Take good care of the one beside you,
Your child, Semetey.
You will flee to Bukhara;
Kanykei, my child, you will take your place.
When the child reaches seven,
Calling him the lamp left by the accomplished one,
Be sure to place him with a mullah.
When the child reaches eight—
Be sure to put a gun into his hands.
Prepare your child.
When he reaches twelve years old,
Weeping and sobbing, tell him your suffering.
The deeds of the six villains—
Tell him the whole truth, leaving nothing out.
